narrativeBlocks.title: After the duel
narrativeBlocks.body: Achilles kills Hector before the walls of Troy — and it is not enough. He pierces the ankles, lashes the body to his chariot, and drags it through the dust around Patroclus's tomb, day after day.

narrativeBlocks.title: A father's impossible errand
narrativeBlocks.body: Priam, king of Troy and father of the dead man, crosses the enemy lines alone at night with a wagon of ransom — into the tent of his son's killer. He kneels and kisses the hands that killed his children.

narrativeBlocks.title: 'Think of your father'
narrativeBlocks.body: Priam does not argue — he asks Achilles to remember Peleus, his own aged father far away who will never see his son return. The two enemies weep together: one for his father and friend, one for his sons.

narrativeBlocks.title: The body goes home
narrativeBlocks.body: Moved by the shared grief, Achilles lifts the old man up, accepts the ransom, and grants twelve days of truce for Hector's funeral. The Iliad ends not with Troy's fall but with a burial.

narrativeBlocks.title: Why the epic ends here
narrativeBlocks.body: The Iliad's final movement is not conquest but compassion — two men bound by loss. The rage that opened the poem dissolves into the recognition that enemies grieve alike.

quiz.prompt: What finally moves Achilles to return Hector's body?

choices.text: The gods threaten him with divine punishment
The ransom of gold outweighs his anger
Priam kneels before him and asks him to think of his own father — shared grief breaks through the rage

quiz.explanation: Priam asks Achilles to think of Peleus, his own father; the two weep together and Achilles releases the body and grants a funeral truce.
